the embolism spreads anisotropically within the ring of Scots pine and that cavitation fatigue is likely to be involved in embolism spread.

(1) embolism spread is highly anisotropic, (2) cavitation fatigue can affect vulnerability to embolisms, (3) prior embolism can affect the vulnerability to embolization and (4) a novel 2D model was developed and validated to simulate the spread in a tracheid-based xylem.
the spread of xylem embolisms in Scots pine is mainly controlled by the tracheid-to-pit air-seeding process and that the presence of embolism can affect the vulnerability of the xylems.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the spread of embolic bubbles in xylem and the role of tracheids in this phenomenon.
the formation and spread dynamics of embolism and their relationship with the anatomical features of xylem.

the development of a novel methodological approach to study embolism spread in tracheids, which is based on the use of X-ray microtomographic images to quantify the embolism spread and the development of a new 2D model to simulate the spread in anisotropic structures.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the vulnerability of the xylems of the species studied here is mainly determined by anatomical traits of the bordered pits and the presence of embolism.
tracheid-to-pit membrane air seeding is a major factor in embolism spread in tracheid-based trees, and that cavitation fatigue is a major factor affecting the resistance to embolation.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the embolism spreading process in Scots pine is highly anisotropic and is strongly dependent on tracheid-to-pit membrane resistance, which is the main factor determining embolism spread in this species.
embolism formation is not the only factor to be considered to understand the spread of embolsim in xylem, but also the micro-morphological traits of pit pairs and the presence of embolism.
the vulnerability to cavitation is highly variable in Scots pine, and that this variability could be linked to anatomical traits.
The main takeaway from our work is that
embolism formation, spread and removal in tracheid-based xylems is a complex process that is highly variable between xylem cells and is not fully understood.
the spread of embolsim in tracheid-based xylem species is strongly influenced by the anisotropy of the xylematic network.
the spread of xylem embolisms is highly variable and depends on the xylem architecture.
